The head is the English name, optionally ', _Latin_', then '.--'. Irregular heads: 'Linnet, _Fringilla cannabina ?_--' (no period), 'Redshank and Sandpiper, _Totanus calidris_.--', 'Rock Birds.--', 'Ducks.--', and group names such as 'Turdidæ.--' and 'Corvidæ.--'. The Gulls note (694-733) quotes a 'Scotsman' story and a letter from Mr. Jack of the Bell Rock. The Gannet note (783-821) is mostly a later Bell Rock schedule from Mr. Jack with records for 5, 18, 19 and 25 Feb and 10 and 17 March 1881 (Larks, Linnets, a Crow, a Snowflake); these are not Gannets. notes:
I read the whole report text from line 1 to line 5050, and I checked the licence text after that by search and spot reads (5330-5363). Line numbers are 1-based, as Read shows them. The 37 sections are consecutive from 1 to 5363 with no gaps or overlaps. Each section starts at its own heading line, and the blank lines before a heading belong to the section above it. Coast is left empty for the Gutenberg and front-matter parts.

Points for a program cutting the report:
(1) The 1880 report has only four coast headings, printed in capitals with a full stop: EAST COAST OF SCOTLAND (133), EAST COAST OF ENGLAND (1118), WEST COAST OF SCOTLAND (2891), WEST COAST OF ENGLAND (3987). There is no Irish coast. Heligoland has no section: Gätke's notes sit inside the East England species entries ('At Heligoland, ...').
(2) The capitalised lines in the contents list (lines 70-93) are not headings; they carry page numbers.
(3) Species heads are the English name, optionally ', _Latin_', then '.--' at the start of a paragraph. Variants occur: ',--' or '?_--', a name without underscores, a missing '--' (East England 2379 Sanderling, 1720, 1941; West England 4115), group heads (Falconidæ., Turdidæ., Anatidæ., Limicolæ., ...), Latin-only heads (Faroe), heads wrapped over two lines (2478-9, 4235-6, 4261-2, 4525-6), and a leading '*' (4892).
(4) '_Note._--' and '_Notes._--' paragraphs (once '_Note,_--' at 3791) belong to the entry above them and usually give other observers' records. Twice a note starts mid-line (3829; 3848 in parentheses).
(5) Footnotes are set inline as '[Footnote n: ...]' blocks, numbered 1-21 through the whole report. Their markers '[n]' sit mid-line, and one is attached to a heading ('SPRING MIGRATION, 1880.[15]', 3002).
(6) Bold headings are wrapped in '=' (947, 1087).
(7) Within an entry, records run on without a break as 'At <Station> L.H./L.V., <date>, ...'. Entries often end with headless summary sentences or paragraphs (e.g. 1897-1910, 4210-4224).
(8) Seasons. East Scotland species (304-829) mix spring and autumn by design. In West Scotland autumn, lines 3761-3860 mix both seasons; I split them out. West England has no season heading; I marked it autumn, apart from a few March and February records.
(9) Station-list quirks. The East Scotland list starts at No. 4. Its footnote marks (†‡§‖¶) after names and heights are not the † 'new station' prefix. The West England numbers 110-148 overlap the West Scotland numbers 110-120, as printed.
(10) Two places in the 'other' parts look like entries but are not: the erratum line (4994) and '_Iceland and Faroe._--' (136), which starts prose.
